reasons: The helpers have no tests of their own, so their correctness is inferred from the tests that use them.
Many sample values are fixed in the builder, so a schema change may need manual updates here.
The sample record builder is long and depends on many schema names, so a rename breaks every test that uses it.

terms.meaning: sample data or a prepared setup that tests use as a starting point
a fake stand-in for a real component that returns preset answers
a part of the system that calls a language model to do one task
the set of source excerpts a run is allowed to cite
the structured description of one analysed business process, including its current steps, future design, and value inputs
the part that combines several process records into one result

used_by: Test files in the test suite (exact paths not visible in this packet)

sections.name: File setup
sections.title: Module purpose and imports
sections.what: The opening description explains that these helpers exist for offline agent tests. It also lists the building blocks used, sets a sample industry description, a sample taxonomy line, and a sample case id used by later helpers.
sections.why: The header explains the decision to test contracts rather than model judgement, and the imports show where each shared piece comes from.
sections.watch_out: The sample case id and industry text feed into prompts and other fixtures, so changing them can change many results.

sections.name: StubUsage
sections.title: Fake token usage counter
sections.what: A stand-in for the usage report that a real model reply carries, with input, output and cache token counts set to fixed defaults.
sections.why: Agents may read usage from a reply, so a stand-in lets them run without a real reply.
sections.watch_out: The defaults are fixed, so budget tests see these numbers unless they override them.

sections.name: StubResponse
sections.title: Fake model reply
sections.what: A stand-in for one model reply, holding a parsed answer and a usage report.
sections.why: It matches the shape the agents expect, so they can be tested without the real model.
sections.watch_out: If the real reply shape changes, this stand-in must change too, or tests will pass against an outdated shape.

sections.name: StubMessages
sections.title: Fake message handler that replays answers
sections.what: Returns the next queued reply for each model request, or raises a queued error. It records every request so tests can inspect what was sent, and it fails the test if the agent asks for more replies than were queued.
sections.why: It lets a test script exactly what the model says and then check what the agent asked for.
sections.watch_out: Replies are used in order, so adding or removing a model call changes which reply each call gets.

sections.name: StubClient
sections.title: Fake model client
sections.what: A fake version of the model connection, with a shortcut to build it from queued replies and a list of every request made.
sections.why: It follows the same interface the agents depend on, so if that interface changes, this stand-in is flagged rather than quietly drifting.
sections.watch_out: It never contacts the network, so a test using it cannot show what the real service would return.

sections.name: evidence_item
sections.title: Sample evidence entry
sections.what: Builds one sample evidence entry with a numbered id, a case corpus source, a page reference, and a chosen authority tier.
sections.why: Gives tests realistic-looking evidence to cite without loading a real corpus.
sections.watch_out: The id numbering pattern is relied on by tests that expect specific ids.

sections.name: evidence_pack
sections.title: Sample evidence pack
sections.what: Builds an evidence pack with a chosen number of sample entries. Zero gives an empty pack, used for the case with no evidence.
sections.why: Tests of how agents handle missing evidence need an empty pack, while other tests need a populated one.
sections.watch_out: The retrieval date and snapshot id are fixed, so any date comparison depends on these values.

sections.name: manifest
sections.title: Sample run manifest
sections.what: Builds a run manifest with a fixed run id, a fixed creation date, and a chosen depth tier, defaulting to defensible.
sections.why: Agents need run details to be present, and fixed values keep tests repeatable.
sections.watch_out: The depth tier is passed through with a type-check override, so this helper does not check that the value is valid.

sections.name: run_context
sections.title: Sample run context bundle
sections.what: Bundles a sample manifest, evidence pack, prompt prefix, and token budget into the context an agent receives. Zero evidence gives the unsupported case, and the budget ceiling is set by the caller.
sections.why: Agents receive these items together, so one helper keeps the tests consistent.
sections.watch_out: The prompt prefix is built from fixed industry and taxonomy text, so prompt tests depend on that text.

sections.name: process_record (part 1)
sections.title: Starting the sample process record
sections.what: Imports the schema pieces needed to hand-build a full process record. This part only gathers the vocabulary the builder uses.
sections.why: The docstring says the record is built by hand so reconciler tests are not affected by failures in the eight agents.
sections.watch_out: The builder imports many schema names. If one is renamed, every test that uses this builder fails to load.

sections.name: process_record (part 2)
sections.title: Scores, current steps and future steps
sections.what: Creates a scorecard in which each dimension takes the given score or defaults to three, a current process with one step, a future state with one agent doing that step, and an exception model with an escalation rule.
sections.why: Likely reason: the smallest valid shape that still has every required part.
sections.watch_out: Every dimension cites the same evidence id, so tests that count evidence may see unexpected totals.

sections.name: process_record (part 3)
sections.title: Value inputs, constraints and data readiness
sections.what: Sets the value inputs such as effort, shares, error rates and ramp months as fixed ranges, with effort supplied by the caller. Adds one regulatory constraint that requires a human to decide, and a data readiness note recording a missing owner.
sections.why: Likely reason: a realistic but minimal set so the value and feasibility code has something to work with.
sections.watch_out: The regulatory constraint sets the autonomy ceiling to human decides, which affects any test about automation level.

sections.name: process_record (part 4)
sections.title: Assembling the full record and its confidence
sections.what: Fills in the implications, value inputs and confidence scores, then assembles the complete process record with a fixed run id. Confidence is computed from the evidence pack rather than typed in.
sections.why: The comment says implications are populated on purpose, so tests about what a critic sees are not checking an empty block.
sections.watch_out: Confidence is calculated from the evidence pack, so changing the pack changes the scores in every record built here.

summary: Provides shared stand-ins and sample data, including a fake model client, sample evidence, a sample run manifest, and a hand-built valid process record, so agent and reconciler tests run offline and predictably.
purpose: Give tests a repeatable way to exercise agents and the reconciler without calling the real model or running the full pipeline.
why: The module header says agent tests check what an agent asks for and how it retries, not the model's judgement. The process record is built by hand so that a failing reconciler test points at the reconciler, not at eight agents.
how: Stub classes stand in for the model connection. They return queued answers in order and record every request. Helper functions create evidence items, evidence packs, a manifest, a run context, and a sample process brief. The largest helper assembles a full process record, computes its confidence from the evidence pack, and returns it.
inputs: Optional arguments on the helpers, such as evidence count, depth tier, shared enabler list, effort figure, and dimension scores. For the stub client, a queue of replies or errors.
outputs: A stub client, sample evidence objects, a run context, a process brief, and a complete sample process record.
risks: The stubs never reach the network or the real pipeline, so passing tests show only the contract, not how the real model behaves. If the real schema changes, the hand-built record may fall out of step and tests may not notice. The stub raises an error when called more times than queued, which can look like an unrelated failure.
debug: If many agent or reconciler tests fail together, look here first, since a schema or interface change may have broken a helper. Check the imports from the schema and agents packages. For a single odd test value, check the arguments passed to the record builder. For the stub, check how many replies the test queued.
